item.title: Krista A. Haapanen
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Krista A. Haapanen

Assistant Professor
Office: Sakamaki C411
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-3695
Email: haapanen@hawaii.edu

Browse My Publications:

Background

I first learned about community psychology during my doctoral program, and I soon found that the associated values, principles, and research approaches were the academic "home" that I had been searching for. Through exposure to participatory and community-engaged research approaches, I learned that academic research can attend both to the practical concerns of people experiencing injustice and to advances in scholarship. I am excited to share my passion for community psychology, especially its commitment to interweaving the practice of research with the efforts, values, priorities, and narratives of people that research has misrepresented and harmed.

Education

  • PhD, Community Research and Action, Vanderbilt University, 2024
  • MS, Community Development, University of California, Davis, 2018
  • BS, Biology, University of Puget Sound, 2014

Courses

  • PSY 280: Introduction to Community Psychology

Research

My research explores the processes by which grassroots and community-based organizations pursue improvements in their communities' health and well-being. I use a community-engaged approach and mixed methods, examining the ways in which these organizations engage citizens in civic activities, build communities' power to shape their futures, and generate lasting changes to community conditions. My work employs a "networked" ecological perspective that illuminates the role of social interaction in human, organizational, and community development, and my approach to scholarship is grounded in dual commitments to rigorous research and the production of actionable insights for use by practitioners, decision-makers, funders, and evaluators of community change efforts.

Background

I first learned about community psychology during my doctoral program, and I soon found that the associated values, principles, and research approaches were the academic "home" that I had been searching for. Through exposure to participatory and community-engaged research approaches, I learned that academic research can attend both to the practical concerns of people experiencing injustice and to advances in scholarship. I am excited to share my passion for community psychology, especially its commitment to interweaving the practice of research with the efforts, values, priorities, and narratives of people that research has misrepresented and harmed.

Education

  • PhD, Community Research and Action, Vanderbilt University, 2024
  • MS, Community Development, University of California, Davis, 2018
  • BS, Biology, University of Puget Sound, 2014

Courses

  • PSY 280: Introduction to Community Psychology

Research

My research explores the processes by which grassroots and community-based organizations pursue improvements in their communities' health and well-being. I use a community-engaged approach and mixed methods, examining the ways in which these organizations engage citizens in civic activities, build communities’ power to shape their futures, and generate lasting changes to community conditions. My work employs a "networked" ecological perspective that illuminates the role of social interaction in human, organizational, and community development, and my approach to scholarship is grounded in dual commitments to rigorous research and the production of actionable insights for use by practitioners, decision-makers, funders, and evaluators of community change efforts.

Background

I first learned about community psychology during my doctoral program, and I soon found that the associated values, principles, and research approaches were the academic "home" that I had been searching for. Through exposure to participatory and community-engaged research approaches, I learned that academic research can attend both to the practical concerns of people experiencing injustice and to advances in scholarship. I am excited to share my passion for community psychology, especially its commitment to interweaving the practice of research with the efforts, values, priorities, and narratives of people that research has misrepresented and harmed.

Education

  • PhD, Community Research and Action, Vanderbilt University, 2024
  • MS, Community Development, University of California, Davis, 2018
  • BS, Biology, University of Puget Sound, 2014

Courses

  • PSY 280: Introduction to Community Psychology

Research

My research explores the processes by which grassroots and community-based organizations pursue improvements in their communities' health and well-being. I use a community-engaged approach and mixed methods, examining the ways in which these organizations engage citizens in civic activities, build communities’ power to shape their futures, and generate lasting changes to community conditions. My work employs a "networked" ecological perspective that illuminates the role of social interaction in human, organizational, and community development, and my approach to scholarship is grounded in dual commitments to rigorous research and the production of actionable insights for use by practitioners, decision-makers, funders, and evaluators of community change efforts.

item.title: Christina Moyer
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Christina Moyer

Instructor
Office: Sakamaki D413
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-2846
Email: christina.moyer@hawaii.edu

Background

My interest in psychology began as an undergraduate at the University of Hawaiʻi, where faculty at both a UH community college and UH Mānoa sparked my curiosity about human behavior and inspired me to pursue a career in psychology. That curiosity has guided 15 years of teaching at community colleges and universities across five states before returning home to Hawaiʻi. I am passionate about making psychology accessible, engaging, and relevant, whether introducing students to the foundations of psychology or exploring the complexities of human sexuality. Above all, I hope students leave my classroom with greater confidence in their ability to succeed and a deeper understanding of how psychology applies to their everyday lives.

Education

  • PhD, Psychology, Montana State University-Bozeman, 2022
  • MA, Psychology, Northern Arizona University, 2013
  • BA, Psychology, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, 2008

Courses

  • PSY 100: Survey of Psychology
  • PSY 352: Psychology of Human Sexuality

Research

What began as an invitation to teach a human sexuality course quickly sparked a lasting interest in the field. My research explores human mating behavior across the full spectrum, from short-term mating to long-term monogamy and everything in between. What drives an individual to select a particular partner or mating style? I examine how evolutionary and sociocultural forces, including gender socialization, shape partner selection, mating strategies, and sexual behavior. Ultimately, I am fascinated by the complexities of how and why humans connect.

Background

My interest in psychology began as an undergraduate at the University of Hawaiʻi, where faculty at both a UH community college and UH Mānoa sparked my curiosity about human behavior and inspired me to pursue a career in psychology. That curiosity has guided 15 years of teaching at community colleges and universities across five states before returning home to Hawaiʻi. I am passionate about making psychology accessible, engaging, and relevant, whether introducing students to the foundations of psychology or exploring the complexities of human sexuality. Above all, I hope students leave my classroom with greater confidence in their ability to succeed and a deeper understanding of how psychology applies to their everyday lives.

Education

  • PhD, Psychology, Montana State University-Bozeman, 2022
  • MA, Psychology, Northern Arizona University, 2013
  • BA, Psychology, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, 2008

Courses

  • PSY 100: Survey of Psychology
  • PSY 352: Psychology of Human Sexuality

Research

What began as an invitation to teach a human sexuality course quickly sparked a lasting interest in the field. My research explores human mating behavior across the full spectrum, from short-term mating to long-term monogamy and everything in between. What drives an individual to select a particular partner or mating style? I examine how evolutionary and sociocultural forces, including gender socialization, shape partner selection, mating strategies, and sexual behavior. Ultimately, I am fascinated by the complexities of how and why humans connect.

Background

My interest in psychology began as an undergraduate at the University of Hawaiʻi, where faculty at both a UH community college and UH Mānoa sparked my curiosity about human behavior and inspired me to pursue a career in psychology. That curiosity has guided 15 years of teaching at community colleges and universities across five states before returning home to Hawaiʻi. I am passionate about making psychology accessible, engaging, and relevant, whether introducing students to the foundations of psychology or exploring the complexities of human sexuality. Above all, I hope students leave my classroom with greater confidence in their ability to succeed and a deeper understanding of how psychology applies to their everyday lives.

Education

  • PhD, Psychology, Montana State University-Bozeman, 2022
  • MA, Psychology, Northern Arizona University, 2013
  • BA, Psychology, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, 2008

Courses

  • PSY 100: Survey of Psychology
  • PSY 352: Psychology of Human Sexuality

Research

What began as an invitation to teach a human sexuality course quickly sparked a lasting interest in the field. My research explores human mating behavior across the full spectrum, from short-term mating to long-term monogamy and everything in between. What drives an individual to select a particular partner or mating style? I examine how evolutionary and sociocultural forces, including gender socialization, shape partner selection, mating strategies, and sexual behavior. Ultimately, I am fascinated by the complexities of how and why humans connect.

item.title: Arkadiy Maksimovskiy
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Arkadiy Maksimovskiy

Assistant Professor
Office: Sakamaki D403
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-6672
Email: arkadiym@hawaii.edu

Browse My Publications:

Background

I grew up in Russia, and later in the Bronx. I am the first in my family to pursue academia, guided by mentors who encouraged me to follow my curiosity. I began college in photography and film, fascinated by how a designed environment (a film set) can tell a meaningful story. A few psychology classes later, I switched: psychology let me build environments (experiments) not just to tell stories, but to discover them. My research began with reward in excess, studying addiction during a PhD at Boston University and a NIDA fellowship at McLean Hospital, and now centers on its absence: an NIMH K01 asking whether mirth restores positive memory in depression. At UH Mānoa, I am excited to extend this work and help students find questions they care about and the tools to answer them.

Education

  • PhD, Behavioral Neuroscience, Boston University, 2017
  • BA, Psychology, Cornell University, 2007

Courses

  • PSY 212: Survey of Research Methods

Research

I am launching the POEM Lab (Positive Emotion Mechanisms) to study how good feelings are built, and why they are harder to induce in the lab than unpleasant ones. Graphic injury distresses nearly everyone, yet a song that thrills one listener leaves the next cold. The usual answer, that positive experience depends more on context, culture, and the person, only renames the puzzle: what makes one thing delightful and another flat? I pursue this and related questions by inducing positive states, especially mirth (the feeling behind laughter), and reading them out with behavioral, computational, and neural measures (e.g., EEG). My goal is to learn what makes a specific person feel good, and how that knowledge might help people who have lost the capacity for pleasure.

Background

I grew up in Russia, and later in the Bronx. I am the first in my family to pursue academia, guided by mentors who encouraged me to follow my curiosity. I began college in photography and film, fascinated by how a designed environment (a film set) can tell a meaningful story. A few psychology classes later, I switched: psychology let me build environments (experiments) not just to tell stories, but to discover them. My research began with reward in excess, studying addiction during a PhD at Boston University and a NIDA fellowship at McLean Hospital, and now centers on its absence: an NIMH K01 asking whether mirth restores positive memory in depression. At UH Mānoa, I am excited to extend this work and help students find questions they care about and the tools to answer them.

Education

  • PhD, Behavioral Neuroscience, Boston University, 2017
  • BA, Psychology, Cornell University, 2007

Courses

  • PSY 212: Survey of Research Methods

Research

I am launching the POEM Lab (Positive Emotion Mechanisms) to study how good feelings are built, and why they are harder to induce in the lab than unpleasant ones. Graphic injury distresses nearly everyone, yet a song that thrills one listener leaves the next cold. The usual answer, that positive experience depends more on context, culture, and the person, only renames the puzzle: what makes one thing delightful and another flat? I pursue this and related questions by inducing positive states, especially mirth (the feeling behind laughter), and reading them out with behavioral, computational, and neural measures (e.g., EEG). My goal is to learn what makes a specific person feel good, and how that knowledge might help people who have lost the capacity for pleasure.

Background

I grew up in Russia, and later in the Bronx. I am the first in my family to pursue academia, guided by mentors who encouraged me to follow my curiosity. I began college in photography and film, fascinated by how a designed environment (a film set) can tell a meaningful story. A few psychology classes later, I switched: psychology let me build environments (experiments) not just to tell stories, but to discover them. My research began with reward in excess, studying addiction during a PhD at Boston University and a NIDA fellowship at McLean Hospital, and now centers on its absence: an NIMH K01 asking whether mirth restores positive memory in depression. At UH Mānoa, I am excited to extend this work and help students find questions they care about and the tools to answer them.

Education

  • PhD, Behavioral Neuroscience, Boston University, 2017
  • BA, Psychology, Cornell University, 2007

Courses

  • PSY 212: Survey of Research Methods

Research

I am launching the POEM Lab (Positive Emotion Mechanisms) to study how good feelings are built, and why they are harder to induce in the lab than unpleasant ones. Graphic injury distresses nearly everyone, yet a song that thrills one listener leaves the next cold. The usual answer, that positive experience depends more on context, culture, and the person, only renames the puzzle: what makes one thing delightful and another flat? I pursue this and related questions by inducing positive states, especially mirth (the feeling behind laughter), and reading them out with behavioral, computational, and neural measures (e.g., EEG). My goal is to learn what makes a specific person feel good, and how that knowledge might help people who have lost the capacity for pleasure.
